say.text: A 2-year-old with known tetralogy of Fallot comes for review. The ECG shows right axis deviation, a prominent R wave in V1 and an upright T wave in V1.
What does this ECG pattern tell you about the ventricles?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Put the axis and lead V1 together. Both findings point to the same side of the heart.
Which ventricle would that be?
Left ventricular hypertrophy is the default guess for a big ventricle, so it is tempting. But TOF does not load the left ventricle.
Right axis deviation with prominent R or qR waves in V1 and upright T in V1 is characteristic of right atrial enlargement and **right ventricular hypertrophy**.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix this one firmly: the hypertrophy in TOF is on the right, secondary to chronic systemic pressures.

say.text: Yes. Right axis deviation, prominent R or qR in V1 and upright T in V1 fit right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy.
The hypertrophy in TOF is of the right ventricle, secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
Same child. The radiologist reports a "boot-shaped" heart with an upturned apex and a concave pulmonary artery segment.
What does the boot shape mean?

choices.label: Normal-sized heart; the apex is upturned by RV hypertrophy
The apex is upturned by left ventricular hypertrophy
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think of the ECG you just read. Whichever ventricle was hypertrophied there is the one that lifts the apex.
And a boot is a shape, not a size.

"Boot" sounds like a big heart, so cardiomegaly is a tempting read. But it describes shape. StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette with an upturned apex and a concave main pulmonary artery segment.
The upturned apex is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy, together with the concave pulmonary arterial segment.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember it this way: boot-shaped does not mean big. The silhouette is described as normal in size.

say.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy is a familiar cause of apical change, so it is tempting. But the ventricle that hypertrophies in TOF is the right one.
The upturned apex of the boot-shaped heart is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the two tests: the ECG and the X-ray both point to the right ventricle.

say.text: Right. The silhouette is normal in size, with an upturned apex and a concave main pulmonary artery segment.
The upturned apex is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy.
The lung fields can also show decreased pulmonary vascular markings, called **pulmonary oligaemia**.
You now have a suggestive ECG and a boot-shaped film. The consultant asks which investigation confirms the diagnosis and is the gold standard.
Your pick?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The ECG and X-ray showed you effects of the lesion on the heart. Which test would let you see the abnormal anatomy itself?
The boot is the most famous picture in TOF, so it is tempting to call the X-ray diagnostic. But it is a classic sign, not the gold standard.
The **echocardiogram** is the gold standard for diagnosis and the primary diagnostic modality.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two ideas: classic sign is the boot, gold standard is the echo.

say.text: RV hypertrophy on ECG fits TOF, so it is tempting to lean on it. But it shows the effect on the ventricle, not the anatomy.
Echocardiography allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy and is the gold standard for diagnosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: for the exam, gold standard investigation for diagnosis is the echocardiogram.

say.text: Yes. The **echocardiogram** is the gold standard for diagnosing TOF.
It allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy and remains the primary modality for diagnosis.
Later the team plans further imaging. They want both anatomical detail and functional information, without ionising radiation.
Which modality fits?
CT is a sensible thought: contrast-enhanced CT is useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology of TOF.
But the modality described as giving both anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation is **MRI**.
The X-ray is where we started, so it is tempting. But it shows the boot-shaped silhouette and vascular markings, not functional information.
**MRI** provides both anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.
Yes. **MRI** gives anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.
Contrast-enhanced **CT** is useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology.

choices.label: Go deeper: what echo may miss

say.text: Even the gold standard has limits. Echocardiography has limitations in assessing associated extracardiac anomalies, such as peripheral pulmonary stenosis and atresia.
CT can also evaluate post-surgical changes, such as patency of palliative shunts.

choices.label: Why does the pulmonary artery matter?

say.text: Detailed pulmonary artery assessment matters because repairing the cardiac defects without addressing pulmonary artery hypoplasia or stenosis has a poor outcome.
The main or right pulmonary artery diameter should be compared with that of the ascending aorta.
One more exam wrinkle: most infants with TOF may not show the boot-shaped finding.
So a normal-looking film does not rule TOF out, and the echo stays the test that settles it.
ECG: right axis deviation, prominent R in V1, right ventricular hypertrophy. X-ray: boot-shaped, upturned apex from RV hypertrophy, normal-size silhouette.
Gold standard: **echocardiography**. MRI and CT add detail.
